title: Loop gain and why feedback helps

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
The **loop gain** \(T\) is the gain around a feedback loop. Break the loop at one point, inject a test signal, and follow it around to where you broke it. The ratio of the returned signal to the injected one is \(-T\) for negative feedback.

In the standard diagram, \(T = af\). In a real system, \(T\) includes every block in the loop: sensor gain, controller, actuator, plant. Because \(T\) depends on frequency, it is usually large at low frequency and falls off at high frequency.

The loop gain sets almost everything. The closed-loop gain is \(\frac{1}{f}\frac{T}{1 + T}\), the error is \(1/(1 + T)\) of the input, and sensitivity to forward-path changes is \(1/(1 + T)\). As a rule, wherever \(|T| \gg 1\) feedback is effective. Where \(|T| \ll 1\), the system behaves as if the loop were open. The crossover where \(|T| = 1\) is where stability is decided.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ T = a f, \qquad S = \frac{1}{1 + T}, \qquad \frac{dA/A}{da/a} = \frac{1}{1 + T} \]
\[ \frac{T}{1 + T} \approx 1 - \frac1T \quad (T \gg 1) \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A loop has a sensor gain of 0.02, a controller gain of 150 and a plant gain of 6. Then \(T = 0.02 \times 150 \times 6 = 18\). The closed-loop gain is \(\frac{1}{0.02}\cdot\frac{18}{19} = 47.4\), and a 10% drop in the plant gain changes it by only about 0.5%.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Leaving one block out of the loop product.
- Breaking the loop without keeping the loading at the break point.
- Treating \(T\) as constant across frequency.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The loop gain's size gives steady-state accuracy, and its phase near crossover gives the stability margins.
